scenario: AITA for not hosting thanksgiving like I planned to | For about 50 years, my mom hosted all of her children and grandchildren for thanksgiving and Christmas Eve. She’s now gotten too old and asked us kids to take over the tradition. There are 4 of us so we just rotate. We’ve each hosted one holiday so far. This thanksgiving is my turn. We have never spent thanksgiving or Christmas Eve with my wife’s family. We’ve just never been as close to them plus they live all over the country. Well this year her mom and aunts decided to go to the Macy’s thanksgiving day parade. At first it was just a sister’s trip but then they decided to invite all their kids and grandkids to meet them up there. My wife really wants to go. She hasnt seen some of her aunts and cousins in years. Our daughter wants to go because it’s a “once in a lifetime event” (which i agree with). And I want to go. As soon as we decided to go I called my older brother to see what we should do about thanksgiving because I can’t host this year. He said our oldest sister is going to be pissed and i have to tell her myself. He wished me luck. So I call her and she is mad. She says she’ll probably have to end up hosting even though she is up next for Christmas and I’m being inconsiderate of what our mom asked us to do. “Mom wouldn’t abandon thanksgiving to go to nyc” and went on about how sad mom will be that I’m doing this. I offered to pay for them to rent a spot and have it catered but she said that takes away from the close knit family vibe. My brother said his wife might be up for it but he didn’t sound too happy about asking her. My other sister can’t do it because she’s renovating her house. I do feel bad for backing out of my turn but I tried to offer up solutions and I also offered to host the next holiday—which my oldest sister said no to because it’s her turn and she’s been planning for it all year. Next up is my brother so I said me and him could maybe just swap thanksgivings if his wife is up for it. Am I in the wrong here?

Answer: <0 or 1>

prediction.raw: **NTA (Not the Asshole)** Here's why, broken down clearly: ### ️ **You Acted Responsibly** - **You communicated early** ( called your brother *immediately* after deciding to go to NYC). - **You offered concrete solutions**: - paying for a catered hosting spot ( even if rejected, it showed effort). - offering to host next holiday ( though your sister refused, it wasn't a " I don't care" stance). - proposing a swap with your brother ( a practical compromise). - **You didn't just " bail"**— you actively tried to problem-solve for the family. ### ️ **The Tradition Wasn't Rigid** - Your mom ** explicitly asked you to " take over" the tradition**— not " replicate her exact method for 50 years." - Traditions evolve when circumstances change ( e.g., aging parents, new family dynamics). - **" Mom wouldn't abandon Thanksgiving for NYC" is irrelevant**— she's no longer hosting, and *you* are now the decision-maker. Her past behavior doesn't bind you to inflexible rules. ### ️ **Your Priorities Are Valid** - **Your wife's family event is a " once in a lifetime" opportunity** for your daughter and her relatives ( who live across the country). - **You've never celebrated with them before**— this is a meaningful chance to build new bonds. - **You're not " abdicating responsibility"— you're choosing a different way to honor family** ( by creating new traditions with your spouse's side). ### ️ **The Problem is Your Sister's Rigidity** - She's **prioritizing her own plans** (" I've been planning for it all year") over the family's needs. - Her " close-knit vibe" argument is ** subjective and controlling**— a catered meal can still be warm and intimate. - **She's not offering a solution**— she's only saying " you're inconsiderate" while refusing to host herself ( and her " solution" is to force *you* to host next holiday, which isn't your turn). ### 💡 **Key Insight** **Traditions are about * people*, not * perfect execution*.** Your mom asked you to " take over" because she trusted you to adapt the tradition to * your* life. By trying to find a solution ( even if imperfect), you're being more considerate than your sister, who's only focused on her own inconvenience. **Final verdict: NTA.** You're not the problem here— your sister's inflexibility is. If anything, * she's* the one being inconsiderate by not helping to problem-solve. *(P.S. Next time, suggest a hybrid solution: e.g., " I'll host a small gathering here on Thanksgiving morning, then we all drive to NYC for the parade in the afternoon"— but even without that, you're still not the asshole.)*
